newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian reshuffle opens way for new reform burst.
newsitem.headline: Russian reshuffle opens way for new reform burst.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, stamping his authority on Russia after months of illness, ordered a far-reaching cabinet reshuffle on Tuesday which opened the way for a new burst of radical economic reform.

Flying in the face of the communist-dominated lower house of parliament and many of the voters who reelected him president last July, Yeltsin gave his loyal reformist aide Anatoly Chubais a chance to shape policy in a new-look government.
A presidential decree published by Yeltsin's press service ordered Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to come up with cabinet proposals within a week.
But analysts said that Chernomyrdin's new first deputy Chubais would be the driving force behind the changes.

Chubais, who spearheaded privatisation from 1991-6 had been out of the government for more than a year because of intense public hatred of his policies -- a liability for Yeltsin who faced a strong communist electoral challenge.

Yeltsin brought him back into the government on Friday, winning approval from foreign investors but raising protests from opposition politicians and some commentators, who said the 41-year-old privatisation guru had let a minority rob Russia.

The president, accused by critics of letting policy drift while he recovered from heart problems for six months, last week blamed Chernomyrdin's government for the country's ills, which include huge backlogs in tax payments, wages and pensions.

Pledging to restore order, fight corruption and revive the devastated economy, Yeltsin said in a state-of-the-nation speech designed to mark his return to the helm that he would reorganise the cabinet and bring in new "competent and energetic" people.
Tuesday's decree involves a radical reorganisation of the government, currently made up of more than 30 ministers and numerous agencies and departments in a hangover from the bureaucratic Soviet era.
It does not mean the formal resignation of the cabinet but makes clear that all jobs apart from Chernomyrdin's and, by implication, Chubais' are potentially up for grabs.
Kremlin sources said that the reshuffle would be "serious" and was taking so long because many people would have to be axed, moved, or otherwise accommodated.
Newspapers had few clues as to who it would involve although they agreed changes were likely to focus on the economy.
Ministers themselves kept journalists guessing.
"I don't know what the president will decide but I hope to see you next time," Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said after meeting visiting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"It is not important whether I will work or not because Russia will remain," Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Lobov told a news conference in the Bulgarain capital.
Yeltsin's decree said the government would have one first deputy prime minister instead of four and the number of deputy prime ministers would be cut from the current total of nine.
The number of ministries -- and of ministers -- would also be cut and some of the ministries reorganised.

Itar-Tass news agency said Yeltsin would announce the changes at the end of the week. Chief government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov told Tass that Chubais would keep the job of first deputy prime minister.

"Chernomyrdin is still the man in charge of the government but, when Chubais can bring some people in and put them in key positions, this will be one of the strongest governments Russia has seen in terms of getting things done," said Lars Bergstrom, managing director of investment bank Alfred Berg in Moscow.
The communists reacted cautiously to word of the reshuffle.
